content: 1. The absence of functional katG is unlikely to result in resistance to isoniazid (INH). Any exceptions to this can be addressed by incorporating them into Group 4 or 5, depending on the quality of the supporting evidence. 2. It is necessary to investigate whether epistasis could interfere with the interpretation of mutations in genes other than Rv0678 and the eis promoter region. For instance, if the mymA operon (Rv3083) is naturally overexpressed in certain isolates, it might counteract a loss-of-function mutation in ethA, although this phenomenon has not been documented to date. 3. The second edition of the mutation catalog was developed using four essential components: High-quality phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) data were manually curated to ensure the best available phenotypic data were used as a reference standard for genotype-phenotype associations. Phenotypic methods were ranked based on WHO endorsement and recency, with WHO-endorsed methods prioritized over non-endorsed ones. Standardized whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data generated using Illumina instruments were included to ensure uniformity in raw sequencing data. These data served as the starting point for bioinformatics analyses. A bioinformatics pipeline was employed to process sequencing data, align reads to the Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv reference genome, and identify variants. This pipeline was optimized to detect single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and small insertions/deletions (indels) up to 15 base pairs in length. It also identified large-scale deletions up to 100 kilobase pairs using an additional open-access tool. A validated algorithmic approach was used to statistically associate genetic variants with phenotypic resistance. Neutral mutations were identified and excluded from further analysis, and isolates with single mutations in candidate genes were analyzed for their association with drug resistance. 4. The computational architecture for the second edition was revised to create a more centralized, efficient, and sustainable workflow. Data and computational processes were transferred to a WHO-supervised cloud service, and a new relational database schema was developed to house data ranging from sequencing information to genotype calls. PostgreSQL was chosen as the database management system, and additional tables were included for studying genetic variants and their phenotypic associations. 5. Data sources for the second edition included legacy datasets from publications, consortium initiatives, and direct submissions in response to public calls for contributions by the WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme. Phenotypic data were collected in tabular formats and integrated into the GenPhenSQL database using Python-based extract-transform-load scripts. Publicly available sequencing data were preferred, but private submissions were accepted if they included raw FASTQ files to ensure uniform bioinformatics processing. 6. Phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) results associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) isolates with available WGS data were collated and analyzed. Intermediate pDST results were converted to binary outcomes (resistant or susceptible) or excluded based on additional grading rules. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) data were also converted into binary results using critical concentrations (CCs) appropriate to the pDST method. 7. pDST data were stratified into four categories based on the level of WHO endorsement: Category 1: Current WHO-endorsed methods, including Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ), Middlebrook 7H10, 7H11, and MGIT, using the latest WHO CCs. Category 2: Previously WHO-endorsed methods, including outdated CCs or unclear adherence to WHO guidelines. Category 3: Other methods, including novel broth microdilution (BMD) plates and methods not endorsed by WHO. Category 4: Excluded results that did not fit into Categories 1–3. 8. To prioritize pDST results, two separate association analyses were conducted: one using data from Categories 1 and 2 (more conservative) and another using data from Categories 1, 2, and 3 (more inclusive). Results were stratified by pDST category and reported in both analyses. When multiple pDST methods were available for the same isolate, the most recent WHO-endorsed method was prioritized. 9. Solid media pDST results were given higher priority than liquid media results within the same category, as liquid media are more likely to miss clinically relevant mutations. Among liquid media methods, MGIT was prioritized over MODS and BACTEC™ 460. Among solid media methods, Middlebrook 7H10 was prioritized over LJ and 7H11.
